entry: Double-reed woodwind instrument. Oboes are usually made of wood, though plastic, resin and hybrid composites are also used. The most common type, the soprano oboe pitched in C, is about 65 cm (25½ in) long, with metal keys, a conical bore and a flared bell. Its bright, penetrating tone carries well over other instruments in large ensembles. Like the [[Bassoon|bassoon]], it uses a double reed, and most professional oboists make their own reeds to control tone and intonation. The oboe is a standard [[Orchestra|orchestral]] and solo instrument, heard in [[Classical music|classical music]], film music and some genres of [[Folk music|folk music]], and occasionally in [[Jazz|jazz]] and popular music. Orchestras tune to a concert A played by the first oboe, because the oboe is the one orchestral instrument that cannot change pitch by moving part of its body. A musician who plays it is called an oboist.

Spherical region of the [[Universe|universe]] containing all [[Matter|matter]] that can be observed from [[Earth]]. Its radius is about 14.26 gigaparsecs (46.5 billion light-years or 4.40×10²⁶ m). The limit comes from the [[Speed of light|speed of light]], not from the capability of technology: the universe has existed for only about 14 billion years, so objects whose light has not yet reached Earth lie beyond the particle horizon. The radius of the visible universe, measured to particles that emitted the [[Cosmic microwave background|cosmic microwave background]], is about 14.0 billion parsecs (about 45.7 billion light-years). Expansion is accelerating, a trend that [[Dark energy|dark energy]] was proposed to explain. Light from objects beyond a comoving distance of about 19 gigaparsecs (62 Gly) will never reach Earth. The total mass of ordinary matter is about 1.5×10⁵³ kg.

Active acquisition of information from a primary source. In living organisms, observation occurs mainly through the senses; in science it often extends to [[Telescope|telescopes]], [[Microscope|microscopes]] and other instruments that detect and record data. Observations are either qualitative, describing characteristics not expressed numerically such as color, texture or behavior, or quantitative, based on counting or measurement. Reproducible observations underpin the [[Scientific method|scientific method]], in which they help formulate and test [[Hypothesis|hypotheses]]. Because unaided perception is limited and prone to errors such as [[Optical illusion|optical illusions]], measurement against a standard unit was developed to produce objective values that different observers can compare.

Research design in which outcomes are measured without the investigator manipulating variables or conditions. Observational studies are commonly used in [[Medicine|medicine]], [[Epidemiology|epidemiology]], [[Psychology|psychology]], sociology and [[Statistics|statistics]]. Unlike a [[Randomized controlled trial|randomized controlled trial]] (RCT), the investigator does not assign subjects to treatment or control groups. Such designs suit situations where a trial would be unethical, impractical or beyond the investigator's control. For example, it would be unethical to assign participants at random to smoke in a trial of whether smoking causes [[Lung cancer|lung cancer]]. Observational studies are susceptible to confounding and [[Bias|bias]], give weaker evidence than RCTs, and cannot on their own establish causality. Common designs include cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies.

Location used for observing terrestrial, marine or celestial events. Observatories have been built for [[Astronomy|astronomy]], climatology, meteorology, geophysics, [[Oceanography|oceanography]] and volcanology. Astronomical observatories may be space-based, airborne, ground-based or underground-based. Most [[Optical telescope|optical telescopes]] are housed in domes and sited far from population centers to avoid light pollution, at high elevations with dark skies, dry air and many clear nights, as in the [[Andes]] and [[Hawaii]]. [[Radio telescope|Radio telescopes]], built since 1933, usually have no domes and can sit in valleys for shielding from interference. Historically, ground-based observatories ranged from a mural instrument to [[Stonehenge]], which has some alignments on astronomical phenomena.

[[Mental disorder|Mental disorder]] marked by intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors (compulsions). Obsessions are persistent unwanted thoughts, images or urges that generate [[Anxiety|anxiety]] or disgust, such as fear of contamination or a need for [[Symmetry|symmetry]]. Compulsions, such as washing, checking or counting, temporarily relieve that distress but reinforce the obsessions. They often take at least one hour a day and impair quality of life. Causes include genetic predisposition, childhood trauma and differences in brain structure and neurotransmitter function, including dysregulation of [[Serotonin|serotonin]], [[Dopamine|dopamine]] and glutamate. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, and the Yale–Brown Obsessive–Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) assesses severity. First-line treatments are exposure and response prevention, [[Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor|selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors]] (SSRIs), or both. Treatment-resistant cases may require second-line drugs or, as a last resort, deep brain stimulation. The disorder is chronic, with periods of severe symptoms and improvement.

Naturally occurring volcanic glass, an [[Igneous rock|igneous rock]]. It forms when silica-rich [[Lava|lava]] cools so quickly that crystals cannot grow. Its high [[Viscosity|viscosity]] slows the diffusion of atoms, inhibiting crystal nucleation. Obsidian consists mainly of [[Silicon dioxide|silicon dioxide]], usually 70% by weight or more, and is usually dark. It is hard and brittle, fracturing into very sharp edges, so it was used for cutting and piercing tools and has been used experimentally as surgical scalpel blades. Because it is not crystalline, it is not a true mineral.

Medical specialty combining two subspecialties: obstetrics and gynecology. Obstetrics covers [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]], [[Childbirth|childbirth]] and the postpartum period, while gynecology covers the health of the [[Female reproductive system|female reproductive system]], including the vagina, uterus, ovaries and breasts. Training is usually combined, although many doctors later specialize in one field. In the [[United States]], certification requires medical school and a four-year residency, adding up to 11–14 years of education and practical experience. In the [[United Kingdom]], training after medical school takes at least nine years, beginning with two years of foundation training. Subspecialties include maternal-fetal medicine, reproductive endocrinology and infertility, and gynecologic oncology.

Enclosed [[Wind instrument|wind instrument]], a type of vessel flute. A typical ocarina has 4 to 12 finger holes and a mouthpiece projecting from the body, and is traditionally made of clay or ceramic. Ocarina-type instruments are believed to date back over 12,000 years and were first made in [[Mesoamerica|Mesoamerican]] and Chinese cultures. The Italian ocarina was invented in 1853 by the 17-year-old Giuseppe Donati, who handmade each one from clay with 7 to 10 finger holes. The 1998 Nintendo 64 game [[The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time|The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time]] featured it.

Philosophical problem-solving principle, also called the principle of parsimony. It recommends that, among explanations, the one constructed from the smallest possible set of elements be preferred. It is often cited as "Entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity," although [[William of Ockham]], a 14th-century English philosopher and theologian, never used those words. Similar ideas appear in [[Aristotle]], and [[Thomas Aquinas]] wrote that it is superfluous to suppose that what can be accounted for by a few principles has been produced by many. [[Isaac Newton]] reformulated it as "nature is pleased with simplicity." In science it serves as an abductive heuristic in building models rather than a rigorous arbiter between them, and it does not choose between [[Hypothesis|hypotheses]] that make different predictions.

[[Romance languages|Romance language]] of southern Europe, also called *lenga d'òc* and sometimes Provençal. It is spoken in southern [[France]], [[Monaco]], Italy's Occitan Valleys and the Val d'Aran in northeast Spain, and is an official language of [[Catalonia]]. It has no single written standard and no official status in France, where most of its speakers live. The [[UNESCO]] Red Book of Endangered Languages classes four of its six major dialects as severely endangered. Its medieval literary tradition includes troubadour [[Poetry|poetry]] from the 11th to 13th centuries.

Esoteric or supernatural beliefs and practices outside the scope of organized religion and science. From Latin *occultus* ('hidden' or 'secret'), the term covers phenomena such as [[Magic (supernatural)|magic]] and [[Mysticism|mysticism]], and paranormal ideas such as extra-sensory perception. In 16th-century Europe, "occult sciences" referred to [[Astrology|astrology]], [[Alchemy|alchemy]] and natural magic. Occultism emerged in 19th-century France and was introduced into English in 1875 by [[Helena Blavatsky]]. Scholars now use the term for esoteric currents that developed in the mid-19th century. It is often applied to traditions such as Theosophy, [[Wicca]] and [[New Age]].

Multidisciplinary field concerned with the safety, health and welfare of people at work. Also called occupational health and safety (OHS), it is related to occupational medicine and occupational hygiene, and it also protects the general public affected by workplace environments. Globally, more than 2.78 million people die each year from workplace-related accidents or diseases, about one death every 15 seconds, and an additional 374 million non-fatal work-related [[Injury|injuries]] occur annually. The economic burden of occupational injury and death is nearly four percent of [[Gross domestic product|global gross domestic product]] each year. In [[Common law|common-law]] jurisdictions, employers have a duty of care to take reasonable care of their employees' safety, and [[Statute|statute law]] may impose further duties and create regulatory bodies. Prevention is addressed through safety and health programs at company level.

Continuous, directed movement of seawater, generated by [[Wind|wind]], the Coriolis effect, temperature and salinity differences and other forces. Surface currents are driven mainly by wind systems, while deep-water currents are driven by differences in [[Density|density]] caused by variations in temperature and salinity. Tides, caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon, also drive currents. Currents are classified as warm or cold and as drifts, currents or streams by velocity. The [[Gulf Stream]], with its extension the North Atlantic Drift, makes northwest Europe far more temperate for its high [[Latitude|latitude]] than other areas at the same latitude. [[Lima]], Peru, has a cooler subtropical [[Climate|climate]] than its tropical surroundings because of the Humboldt Current. The largest is the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, which flows clockwise around [[Antarctica]].

Type of passenger ship used mainly for transportation across seas or oceans. Unlike a [[Cruise ship|cruise ship]], it must carry passengers between continents on a fixed schedule, so it is faster and has a higher hull, a longer bow, thicker plating and a deeper draft. The first were built in the mid-19th century, and rivalry among the [[United Kingdom]], the [[German Empire]] and, to a lesser extent, [[France]] drove larger, faster designs. Long-distance aircraft made them largely obsolete after [[World War II]]. Queen Mary 2, introduced in 2004, is the only ship still in service as an ocean liner.

Large ray-finned fish, *Mola mola*, the type species of its genus. Adults typically weigh between 247 and 1,000 kg (545 and 2,205 lb). Sunfish can be as tall as they are long, between 175 and 180 centimeters (5.74 and 5.91 ft) with fins extended. It is native to tropical and temperate waters worldwide, and its flattened body resembles a fish head without a tail. It was formerly misidentified as the heaviest bony fish, a title that belongs to the closely related *Mola alexandrini*. Its name refers to sunbathing at the surface. Adults have few natural predators, but [[Sea lion|sea lions]], [[Orca|orcas]] and [[Shark|sharks]] eat them. Sunfish are considered a delicacy in [[Japan]], [[Korea]] and [[Taiwan]], and the [[European Union]] bans sales of fish products from the family Molidae. They are frequently caught in gillnets.

Long, narrow depression of the sea floor, typically 50 to 100 km (30 to 60 mi) wide. Trenches lie 3 to 4 km (1.9 to 2.5 mi) below the surrounding floor and can extend thousands of kilometers. About 50,000 km (31,000 mi) of them exist, mostly around the [[Pacific Ocean]]. They mark convergent [[Plate tectonics|plate boundaries]], where oceanic lithosphere sinks beneath another plate. The deepest point, the [[Challenger Deep]] in the [[Mariana Trench]], lies 10,994 m (36,070 ft) below sea level. Trenches generally lie about 200 km (120 mi) from a volcanic arc. Fluid trapped in subducting sediments returns to the surface at trenches, supporting unique [[Biome|biomes]] based on chemotrophic microorganisms. Unlike troughs, which have flat bottoms, trenches have a V-shaped profile.

Earth science devoted to the scientific study of the ocean. Also called oceanology, sea science or marine science, it draws on physics, chemistry, biology and geology. Topics include [[Ocean current|ocean currents]], waves, geophysical fluid dynamics, chemical fluxes across the ocean's boundaries, ecosystem dynamics, and [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]] and seabed geology. Oceanographers also draw on astronomy, geography, hydrology and meteorology. Early exploration was mainly for [[Cartography|cartography]] and limited to surfaces, but the Portuguese campaign of Atlantic navigation became an early systematic project, sustained over many decades, that studied the currents and winds of the Atlantic. The HMS Challenger expedition of 1872–1876 measured depths, temperatures and salinities along global routes.

Medium-sized spotted wild cat, *Leopardus pardalis*, native to the southwestern United States, Mexico, Central and South America and the [[Caribbean]] islands of Trinidad and Margarita. Adults reach 40–50 cm (16–20 in) at the shoulders and weigh between 7 and 15.5 kg (15 and 34 lb) on average. Efficient climbers, leapers and swimmers, ocelots prey on small mammals such as [[Armadillo|armadillos]] and [[Opossum|opossums]], mostly at twilight and night. They are solitary and territorial, and females give birth to one to three kittens. Rated Least Concern by the IUCN, the species is threatened by habitat destruction, hunting and traffic accidents.

Family of natural clay earth pigments made of ferric oxide mixed with clay and sand. Colors range from yellow to deep orange or brown. Red ocher takes its tint from [[Hematite|hematite]], an iron oxide. Sienna and umber contain manganese, which makes them darker. Ocher is one of the earliest human pigments: its processing in Africa dates to around 300,000 years ago, broadly coinciding with the emergence of *Homo sapiens*, and its use in Australia dates to around 50,000 years ago. Clays colored with iron oxide from [[Tin|tin]] and [[Copper|copper]] extraction may also be called ocher.

Standard measure of a fuel's resistance to knocking in an [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]]. A higher octane number means the fuel can withstand more compression before auto-igniting. It does not indicate energy content or power output, which depend on engine design. Higher-octane fuel suits high-compression [[Gasoline|gasoline]] engines, while [[Diesel engine|diesel engines]] use fuels with lower octane and higher cetane numbers. The octane rating of aviation fuel was crucial to aircraft engines in [[World War II]]. Tetraethyl [[Lead|lead]] additives raised ratings from the 1920s, but were phased out in the [[United States]] from 1973 to 1996.

American actress and author. Her breakthrough came in the 2011 drama *The Help*, in which she played a maid in 1960s Mississippi and won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. She was later nominated in the same category for *Hidden Figures* (2016) and *The Shape of Water* (2017), becoming the first Black actress to achieve two consecutive nominations for it. Her other awards include a Primetime Emmy Award, a British Academy Film Award and a Golden Globe Award. She has [[Dyslexia|dyslexia]] and has written the children's series *Randi Rhodes, Ninja Detective*.

Mexican poet, philosopher and diplomat. Born near [[Mexico City]] into a liberal political family, he was awarded the 1990 Nobel Prize in Literature and the 1981 Miguel de Cervantes Prize. In 1937 he attended the Second International Writers' Congress, held in Spain, and showed solidarity with the Republican side against forces led by [[Francisco Franco]]. In Paris he encountered the [[Surrealism|surrealist]] movement, which left a profound impact on him. He joined the Mexican diplomatic service and was ambassador to [[India]] from 1962 to 1968, resigning in 1968 to protest the government's suppression of student protests in Tlatelolco Square. His essay *El laberinto de la soledad* (1950) examines the Mexican national character. He founded the literary magazine *Vuelta* in 1976.

Coordinated armed incursions and massacres in southern Israel by [[Hamas|Hamas]] and other Palestinian militant groups in 2023. On October 7, militants from the blockaded [[Gaza Strip|Gaza Strip]] breached the Gaza–Israel barrier and attacked military bases and civilian communities. At the Nova music festival, 364 civilians were killed, and 251 people were taken hostage to the Gaza Strip. Numerous sources report dozens of cases of rape and sexual assault. Hamas said the attack responded to Israeli occupation and the blockade of Gaza. Governments of 44 countries denounced it as [[Terrorism|terrorism]], and Israel launched a major military operation in Gaza in response.

Second of two 1917 revolutions in Russia, led by [[Vladimir Lenin|Lenin]]'s [[Bolsheviks]]. It followed the February Revolution, which had led to the abdication of [[Nicholas II]]. Bolshevik forces began an insurrection in Petrograd (now [[Saint Petersburg]]) on 7 November 1917 [O.S. 25 October] and captured the Winter Palace on 26 October [N.S. 8 November], toppling the Provisional Government. [[Leon Trotsky]]'s Petrograd Soviet had backed the uprising. It precipitated the [[Russian Civil War]]. The Soviet Union celebrated it as the triumph of the working class; Western observers saw a totalitarian coup.
